Why only two ingredients?
Founder Sidney Frank and cellar master François Thibault built Grey Goose around the idea that a vodka's quality comes entirely from its wheat and water — so the recipe deliberately excludes any additives, flavourings, or sugar.

Why is it called "One Source"?
All the wheat and water used to make Absolut comes from the Åhus area of southern Sweden, and every step from growing the grain to bottling happens in one place — the company's own term for this is "One Source."
What makes continuous distillation different?
Founder Lars Olsson Smith introduced it to Sweden in 1879, distilling the spirit far more times than the standard three or four pot-still passes used elsewhere at the time, for a purer, more consistent result.
Why is there a man's portrait on the bottle?
That's Lars Olsson Smith himself, nicknamed "the Vodka King" in Sweden — his medallion has appeared on every bottle since the brand's earliest days.

Questions

What makes Tennessee whiskey different from bourbon?
Both start from a similar corn-forward mash, but Tennessee whiskey is filtered through sugar maple charcoal before ageing — the Lincoln County Process. That step softens the spirit and gives Jack Daniel's its signature smooth character.
How should I store an opened bottle?
Keep it upright, out of direct sunlight, at room temperature. An opened bottle holds its character well for a year or more if the cap stays tight.
Is Jack Daniel's gluten-free?
Distillation removes gluten proteins, so the finished spirit contains none by the time it's bottled — though as a grain-derived product it isn't formally labelled gluten-free in every market.

title: Johnnie Walker Black Label 12 Year Whisky 70cl
descriptionHtml:
Blended Scotch Whisky · Est. 1820

Forty years before it had a name, it had a promise: consistency, whisky after whisky, blend after blend. Johnnie Walker Black Label is that promise, twelve years in the making.

John Walker began blending in a small grocer's shop in Kilmarnock, Ayrshire, in 1820. What started as a way to smooth out the inconsistency of single malt casks became the foundation of the world's most travelled Scotch. Black Label carries that founding idea forward — single malt and grain whiskies from across Scotland, each held back until it reaches at least twelve years old, before they're allowed anywhere near the blend.

Awards

🏆Gold — International Wine & Spirit Competition 🏆Gold — San Francisco World Spirits Competition 🏆Gold — International Spirits Challenge

Tasting Profile

Nose

Rich and rounded — sweet vanilla up front, giving way to orange peel, dried raisin, and a background of gentle spice.

Palate

Full and smooth. The sweetness carries through, joined by baked fruit and a warming layer of smoke that never overpowers it.

Finish

Long, with lingering peat, malt, and a final wisp of smoke — the signature of the peated malts at its core.

Questions

Why is Black Label's age statement unusual?
Most blended whiskies state the age of only the youngest component. Black Label's 12-year statement applies to every single malt and grain whisky in the blend — a stricter standard than most competitors at this price point.
Is Black Label smoky?
Yes, moderately. Peated malts including Lagavulin and Talisker sit at its core, giving a background smokiness that builds through the palate into the finish, without dominating the sweeter, fruitier notes.
How should I serve it?
Neat or with a single large ice cube to open up the aromatics. It also holds its own in a classic Whisky Highball or Old Fashioned.

descriptionHtml:

Only around one cask in ten thousand carries the character to be bottled as Blue Label.

Introduced in 1992 as the summit of the Johnnie Walker range, Blue Label is a recreation of the earliest, rarest blends the Walker family once made. It draws on some of the scarcest whiskies held in the Johnnie Walker reserves — including stock from distilleries that have long since fallen silent. There is no age statement, because every component is chosen for its character rather than its years. Each bottle is individually numbered.

Why is there no age statement?
Blue Label is blended for character, not calendar. Its whiskies are hand-selected from rare reserves for how they taste — some very old, some less so — so a single age number would misrepresent what is in the bottle.

Questions

What makes the production method special?
Instead of blending white champagne with a little still red wine, the common shortcut, Laurent-Perrier macerates whole Pinot Noir grapes with their skins for 48–72 hours before pressing — a slower, more demanding process that draws out real colour and genuine red-fruit aroma rather than just tinting the wine.
Why is 1968 significant?
That's when Bernard de Nonancourt introduced Cuvée Rosé, treating rosé as its own serious wine rather than a lesser variation of the house's white champagne — a decision that's made it the reference point most other rosé champagnes are still compared to.

It's inspired by a flask design associated with King Henri IV, giving Cuvée Rosé one of the most recognisable silhouettes in Champagne.

descriptionHtml:

The Vodka

Narez is a small-batch British vodka made from organic sugar beet grown on British land. Sugar beet is an unusual base for vodka — most producers use grain or potato — and it is a large part of why this one drinks the way it does: rounder and softer than a grain spirit, without the peppery bite.

Distilled by British distillers and ethically produced from organically farmed ingredients, it is clean on the palate with a smooth, almost creamy finish. That texture makes it as good neat and chilled as it is in a Martini, where a vodka’s mouthfeel is exposed with nowhere to hide.

title: Macallan 18 Year Old Sherry Oak – 70cl
descriptionHtml:
Speyside · Single Malt · 18 Years Old

Macallan 18 Sherry Oak — eighteen years in hand-picked sherry-seasoned casks from Jerez. Mature oak, ginger and raisin.

Single Malt Whisky18 Year OldSherry Oak70cl43% ABV2023 Release
⭐ Instant delivery across Greater London in 30–45 minutes
⭐ Open 24/7 — every day of the year

The Whisky

Macallan’s reputation rests to a remarkable degree on wood. The distillery has long treated cask selection as the decisive factor in a whisky’s character, and Sherry Oak is the clearest expression of that philosophy: matured exclusively in hand-picked sherry-seasoned oak casks from Jerez, Spain, for a full eighteen years.

The result is full-bodied and deeply coloured, with the rich, dried-fruit signature that sherry maturation gives. Mature oak, ginger and raisin lead, layered over the depth and complexity that only long ageing produces. This is the 2023 release, bottled at 43%.

Tasting Notes

NoseMature oak and dried fruit with warm spice.
PalateFull-bodied and rich — mature oak, ginger and raisin, layered and complex.
FinishLong, with lingering oak and spice.

Serve with: dark chocolate, dried fruit and nuts, aged hard cheeses, or on its own after dinner.

At a Glance

Brand The Macallan
Expression 18 Year Old Sherry Oak
Type Single Malt Scotch Whisky
Age 18 years
Cask Sherry-seasoned oak from Jerez, Spain
Release 2023
Alcohol Content 43%
Bottle Size 70cl
Body Full-bodied

Questions

What does “sherry-seasoned” mean?

The casks are made from oak and seasoned with sherry in Jerez before being filled with whisky. That seasoning is what gives the dried-fruit, spice and deep colour character.

How should I serve it?

Neat in a tulip glass, or with a few drops of water to open the aromatics. No ice — it mutes the fruit.

Does the age statement matter?

It guarantees every drop in the bottle has spent at least eighteen years in cask, which is where the depth and layered complexity come from.

descriptionHtml:
Pomerol · Bordeaux · Old Vines

Château du Domaine de L’Eglise 2019 — 98% Merlot from 60- to 70-year-old vines on Pomerol’s gravelly clay.

Red WinePomerol2019 Vintage75cl98% MerlotOld Vines

The Wine

Château du Domaine de L’Eglise is one of Pomerol’s oldest estates, working a compact seven-hectare vineyard of gravelly clay planted with vines now sixty to seventy years old. Old vines yield less and concentrate more, and on Pomerol’s clay that translates into the depth and silky texture the appellation is known for.

The 2019 is 98% Merlot with 2% Cabernet Franc, aged up to 18 months in French oak, 40% of it new. It opens with layers of dark fruit, wild berries and warming spice, then unfolds across a silky, beautifully textured palate held by firm, polished tannins. Leather, vanilla, coffee and oak add earthy sophistication, and the finish stays juicy and balanced rather than heavy.

Tasting Notes

NoseDark fruits and wild berries with warming spice, leather and vanilla.
PalateSilky and beautifully textured — dark fruit with coffee, oak and earthy depth over polished tannin.
FinishJuicy, smooth and remarkably balanced.

Serve with: grilled or roasted red meats, mature cheeses, or rich savoury dishes.

At a Glance

Wine Type Red Wine
Grape Variety Merlot (98%), Cabernet Franc (2%)

Why do old vines matter?

Older vines naturally produce smaller crops of more concentrated fruit, and their deeper roots cope better with weather extremes — both of which show up as depth in the glass.

Drink now or cellar?

Both. The 2019 is approachable with a decant, and the structure supports several more years of development.

How long should I decant it?

Around an hour, served at 16–18°C.

descriptionHtml:
Siberia · Russia · Super-Premium Vodka

VodkaGold Line70cl40% ABVLimited EditionGift-Ready

The Vodka

Beluga Gold Line is made at the Mariinsk distillery in Siberia from malt spirit and pure artesian spring water, then taken through a meticulous five-stage filtration and left to rest for a full ninety days. That resting period is unusual — most vodka goes from still to bottle in a fraction of the time — and it is what gives the spirit its rounded, settled character.

The presentation matches the contents. Each bottle carries a hand-attached metal beluga sturgeon emblem and is sealed with wax, opened ceremonially with the hammer and brush supplied alongside it. Often presented in a leather case, it is a bottle designed to be given as much as poured.

Tasting Notes

NoseClean and refined, with subtle vanilla and honey.
PalateCrisp and smooth — vanilla, honey and a hint of spice.
FinishClean and elegant.

Serve with: neat and chilled, over ice, or as the base of a premium cocktail — caviar, smoked salmon and cured fish are the traditional accompaniments.

Brand Beluga
Expression Gold Line

Distillery Mariinsk, Siberia
Base Malt spirit and artesian spring water
Filtration Five-stage
Resting 90 days
Alcohol Content 40%

Questions

What are the hammer and brush for?

The bottle is sealed with wax. The hammer chips the seal and the brush sweeps away the fragments — a deliberately ceremonial way to open it.

Why rest vodka for 90 days?

An extended rest after blending lets the spirit settle and integrate, which shows as a smoother, rounder texture in the glass.

How should I serve it?

Well chilled, neat or over ice, in a small glass. Its texture is the point, so avoid burying it in a heavy mixer.

descriptionHtml:
Provence · France · Prestige Rosé

Garrus 2022 — old-vine Grenache and Rolle, eleven months in French oak. The wine that proved rosé could be serious.

The Wine

Garrus is the top of Château d’Esclans’s range and Sacha Lichine’s statement wine — the bottling that did most to change how the world thinks about Provence rosé. It comes from old-vine Grenache and Rolle (Vermentino), fruit that yields little and concentrates hard.

What sets it apart is the ageing: eleven months in French oak barrels, unusual for any rosé and unheard of for most. That time in wood builds genuine depth, complexity and structure, so the wine drinks less like a summer refresher and more like a fine white Burgundy — red fruit and citrus framed by subtle oak, with real length.

FinishLong, refined and structured.

Because the fruit can carry it. Old-vine concentration plus barrel ageing produces a rosé with the depth and structure normally associated with serious white wine.

descriptionHtml:

The Gin

Portofino Dry Gin is made in Liguria, on the stretch of coast that gives it its name, and it tastes like it. Twenty-one botanicals go into the bottle — juniper, lemons, lavender, rosemary, marjoram, sage, iris and rose among them — many of them organically grown and handpicked locally rather than shipped in.

Distillation happens in an antique copper pot still using vacuum techniques, which keeps the delicate herbal aromatics intact rather than cooking them off. There are no added sugars and no artificial flavours: what you get is the Ligurian hillside, in a glass.

descriptionHtml:

The Vodka

Tito’s is made in Austin, Texas, from 100% corn — not wheat, not potato — and distilled six times in old-fashioned pot stills rather than the towering column stills most large vodka brands rely on. Every batch is taste-tested before it leaves, which is where the “handmade” in the name comes from.

The corn base and the pot-still method are what give it its character: noticeably smooth, with a clean finish and none of the harsh bite that puts people off cheaper vodka. The distillery also runs Love, Tito’s, which supports non-profits working in disaster relief, community building and animal welfare.

Tasting Notes

NoseClean and neutral with a faint sweetness from the corn.
PalateSmooth and rounded, gentle corn sweetness, no burn.
FinishClean and short — exactly what a mixing vodka should do.

Serve with: a Bloody Mary, a Transfusion, or simply soda and lime. It is a mixing vodka first and foremost.

Base 100% corn
Distillation Six times, old-fashioned pot stills

Production Batch-made, each batch taste-tested

It is distilled from corn rather than wheat or rye. If you have a medical reason to avoid gluten, check the current label or the producer directly.

The Wine

Ridgeview has been making sparkling wine on the South Downs since 1995, and this family-owned Sussex estate is one of the names that established England as a serious sparkling region. The Blanc de Blancs is made exclusively from 100% estate-grown Chardonnay — hand-harvested, whole-bunch pressed, with primary fermentation in stainless steel, then secondary fermentation in bottle and a minimum four years ageing on lees in underground cellars. The 2016 was an exceptional vintage here: a cool spring, smaller yields and a long, sunny ripening period gave concentrated fruit intensity with the vibrant natural acidity that cool-climate English Chardonnay does better than almost anywhere. Most white rum is unaged or barely aged. Planas is not: Diplomático ages it for approximately six years in oak barrels, building genuine complexity, depth and texture, then puts it through meticulous charcoal filtration to strip the colour back out and return it to crystal clarity.

What survives the filtration is the flavour. At 47% ABV this carries intense layers of vanilla, tropical fruit, subtle spice, toasted oak and creamy caramel over a smooth, velvety mouthfeel — the character of an aged rum in a format that behaves like a white. Charcoal filtration after ageing removes the colour picked up from the barrel while leaving most of the flavour behind. That is the whole trick of Planas.

It stands up to mixing. Where a 37.5% white rum can disappear behind lime and sugar, Planas keeps its character in a Daiquiri or Mojito.

The Gin

Gordon’s was first distilled in London in 1769 by Alexander Gordon, and for most of the intervening centuries it has been the benchmark against which other London Dry gins are measured. This is a bottling from the 1950s, sealed with the spring cap closure typical of that era — the format alone dates it.

It is bottled at 40% ABV in the 75cl imperial quart format, from the traditional recipe: dominant juniper berries with coriander seed, angelica root, liquorice, orris root and subtle citrus peels. The closure used on Gordon’s bottles of that period, before modern screw caps. It is one of the clearest ways to date a bottle to the 1950s.

The Gin

Anty Gin is a collaboration between The Cambridge Distillery and the Nordic Food Lab, and it is exactly what the name suggests: the world’s first gin to use ants as a botanical. The essence of precisely 62 Formica rufa — red wood ants, from Danish forests — is distilled into every bottle.

The ants are not a stunt. Formica rufa produce formic acid, and here that replaces the traditional citrus peels entirely, giving a bright, lemony acidity and a tangy citrus lift that no fruit peel quite reproduces. It is produced in extremely small batches, because harvesting ants is exactly as labour-intensive as it sounds.

Formica rufa produce formic acid, which reads as a bright, sharp, lemony acidity. It stands in for the citrus peel that most gins rely on.

Every bottle requires 62 individually harvested ants. The process does not scale, which is why batches are tiny and the gin is a collector’s piece.

NEFT is made in Austria from exactly two ingredients: non-GMO ancient rye grains from Central Europe, and mineral-rich spring water drawn from a mountain aquifer in Golling. That is the whole recipe. The Vodka

Belvedere 10 is the house’s ultra-luxury expression, made as an homage to the original 1910 vodka-making process. It is produced annually in small batches from a single harvest of organic Dankowskie Diamond Rye, grown in one field on the Bartężek estate in north-east Poland, with pure local water.

The spirit is distilled four times in column stills, filtered through cellulose, and then rested for exactly ten months in steel vats. That resting period is the point: it lets the flavours marry into the velvety smoothness the bottling is known for. The result is opulent and multi-faceted, without a hard edge anywhere. Presented in a gift box.

Tasting Notes

NoseCoconut, cacao and vanilla with fresh lemon and subtle almond.
PalateCreamy and opulent — honey, caramel, green coffee, dark chocolate, praline and gentle white pepper, in a flawless silky texture.
FinishLong, elegant and honed, with lingering nutty praline and rich cacao.

Serve with: nothing — neat or over ice is how this is meant to be drunk. It also elevates a premium cocktail if you are inclined.

Questions

Why rest vodka for ten months?

Resting in steel lets the components integrate. Nothing is added and no colour is picked up — the spirit simply becomes rounder and softer than it would be bottled straight off the still.

What does single-field sourcing achieve?

Consistency and traceability. Every bottle in a given release comes from one harvest of one field, so the character of that year’s rye carries through unchanged.

Is it worth drinking neat?

Very much so. The whole design of this vodka — the resting, the single-estate rye — is aimed at a spirit you sip rather than mix away.

Absolut Elyx is made exclusively from winter wheat grown on a single estate in Åhus, southern Sweden — everything from seed to bottle happens within a fifteen-mile radius. That tight geography is unusual for a vodka at any price, and it is the foundation of the whole product.

title: Noilly Prat Vermouth Dry 75Cl
descriptionHtml:
Marseillan · France · Dry Vermouth

Noilly Prat Original Dry — the original French vermouth, aged outdoors in oak by the Mediterranean since 1813.

VermouthMarseillan, FranceSince 181320 Herbs & SpicesOutdoor Oak Ageing18% ABV75cl
⭐ Instant delivery across Greater London in 30–45 minutes
⭐ Open 24/7 — every day of the year

The Vermouth

Noilly Prat has been made in the port town of Marseillan on the French Mediterranean coast since 1813, and the method has not been rationalised since. Carefully selected local white wines are aged outdoors in oak casks — exposed to sun, sea air and the changing seasons — before being macerated with a secret blend of twenty herbs and spices sourced from around the world.

The other signature is dodinage, the hand-stirring process that marries the wine and the botanicals. Between that and the maritime influence, the result is a vermouth of real complexity: dry, elegant, with a saline thread that no indoor-aged vermouth reproduces. At 18% ABV, it is the classic Martini vermouth.

Tasting Notes

NoseChamomile and citrus peel with gentle spice.
PalatePale golden and refined — dry, aromatic and complex, with subtle bitterness.
FinishClean and dry, with a lingering herbal edge.

Serve with: gin, in a proper dry Martini. Equally good chilled over ice as an aperitif, alongside seafood, or used in the kitchen to lift a sauce.

At a Glance

Category Dry Vermouth
Origin Marseillan, South of France
Established 1813
Base Selected local white wines
Ageing Outdoors in oak casks, exposed to the elements
Botanicals Secret blend of 20 herbs and spices
Process Dodinage — hand stirring
ABV 18%
Bottle Size 75cl

Questions

Do I need to refrigerate it after opening?

Yes. Vermouth is a wine-based product and will oxidise. Keep it in the fridge and use it within a few weeks for the best flavour.

What does outdoor ageing do?

The casks sit exposed to sun, sea air and temperature swings. That slow, uneven maturation is what gives Noilly Prat its distinctive dry, slightly saline complexity.

How much goes in a Martini?

Anywhere from a rinse to a full part depending on your taste. Given the quality here, it is worth being generous enough to actually taste it.

title: Aisakura Junmai Daiginjo Sake 72cl
descriptionHtml:
Japan · Junmai Daiginjo · Aiyama Rice

Aisakura Junmai Daiginjo — Aiyama rice, the “Diamond of Sake Rice”, polished to 35%.

SakeJapanJunmai DaiginjoAiyama Rice35% Polishing Ratio72cl
⭐ Instant delivery across Greater London in 30–45 minutes
⭐ Open 24/7 — every day of the year

The Sake

Aisakura is made with Aiyama rice — a rare strain derived from the legendary Yamada-Nishiki, and known among brewers as the “Diamond of Sake Rice”. It is difficult to grow and difficult to work with, which is why so little of it is planted.

Here it is polished to a 35% ratio, meaning 65% of each grain is milled away before brewing begins, leaving only the starchy heart. That is well beyond what Junmai Daiginjo requires, and it is what produces this sake’s clarity: rich and elegant, with a clean sweetness and a refined aroma, refreshing on the palate with a gentle lingering acidity holding it in balance.

Tasting Notes

NoseRefined and elegant.
PalateRich yet clean, with a pleasant sweetness and a refreshing character.
FinishGentle lingering acidity, giving balance and structure.

Serve with: delicate seafood and sushi, or richer dishes. It can be served chilled, at room temperature, or gently warmed — and it is well worth sipping on its own.

At a Glance

Category Junmai Daiginjo Sake
Origin Japan
Rice Aiyama, derived from Yamada-Nishiki
Polishing Ratio 35%
Serving Chilled, room temperature, or gently warmed
Bottle Size 72cl

Questions

What does a 35% polishing ratio mean?

65% of each rice grain is milled away, leaving 35% — the pure starchy centre. Less protein and fat means a cleaner, more refined sake. Junmai Daiginjo requires 50% or below; this goes considerably further.

What is Junmai Daiginjo?

The top grade of sake: made with only rice, water, koji and yeast, with no added brewing alcohol, and highly polished rice. Junmai means pure rice; Daiginjo refers to the milling.

Should I serve it warm or cold?

Chilled is the usual choice for a Daiginjo and shows the aromatics best, but this one is versatile enough to take gentle warming if you prefer.

Sébastien Cathiard took over the family domaine in 2011 and has since made it one of the most talked-about estates in Burgundy. The 12.5 hectares are farmed biodynamically, and the wines are aged over two winters in barrel rather than the usual one — a slower approach that builds complexity and finesse.

Aux Chaumes sits on shallow clay soils over a hard limestone base, and that geology reads directly in the glass as freshness and minerality. The 2022 is rich but lively, and it is the kind of Hautes Côtes de Nuits that makes you question the hierarchy: it drinks well above its classification.

What is Hautes Côtes de Nuits?

The higher, cooler hills sitting behind the famous Côte de Nuits villages. Historically a value appellation, and increasingly a source of serious wine as growers like Cathiard work it properly.

descriptionHtml:

Violot-Guillemard La Platière 2022 — organic Pommard 1er Cru, vinified in ceramic spheres for purity.

The Wine

Domaine Violot-Guillemard is run by Joannes Violot-Guillemard, the fifth generation of his family in Pommard, and it is one of the appellation’s rising names. The estate covers eight hectares, is certified organic, and is known for an unusual technique: vinification in small ceramic spheres, which are neutral in a way oak is not and produce wines of notable purity and precision.

La Platière sits in the heart of the Pommard appellation on clay-limestone soils with Jurassic marls, giving the wine structure and minerality. The 2022 is 100% Pinot Noir and finds a genuinely difficult balance: supple and delicate on the one hand, lively, fresh and complex on the other.

Tasting Notes

NoseVibrant red fruit with floral notes.
PalateSupple and delicate yet lively and complex, with refined tannins and clear minerality.
FinishFresh and precise.

Serve with: duck, game birds, veal or mushroom dishes. Best enjoyed from 2026 to 2033.

At a Glance

Producer Domaine Violot-Guillemard (Joannes Violot-Guillemard)
Appellation Pommard 1er Cru, Burgundy
Vineyard La Platière — clay-limestone with Jurassic marls
Vintage 2022
Grape 100% Pinot Noir
Estate 8 hectares, certified organic

Questions

Why ceramic rather than oak?

Ceramic is neutral — it adds no flavour and allows a small amount of oxygen exchange. The result is a wine that tastes of its vineyard rather than its vessel.

What is Pommard known for?

Structure. Pommard produces the firmest, most tannic reds of the Côte de Beaune. This bottling is a more delicate reading of that, without losing the backbone.

Is 1er Cru worth the step up?

Premier Cru vineyards are individually classified sites with a track record of producing better wine. La Platière sits at the heart of the appellation and shows it.

descriptionHtml:

The Cognac

Hennessy Paradis is a blend of 100 hand-selected eaux-de-vie, slowly matured in oak. That number is the point: each component is chosen individually, and the assembly is the work of the cellar master rather than a formula. The half-bottle format offers the same blend in a more intimate measure.

What emerges is silky and deeply layered, with a restraint that separates it from showier cognacs. Honey, truffle and dried rose petal give way to a long finish touched with cinnamon and cardamom. Made in France, at 40% ABV.

NoseHoney and truffle with dried rose petal.

Spirit Cognac
Origin France
Composition 100 hand-selected eaux-de-vie
Maturation Slowly matured in oak
ABV 40%
Bottle Size 35cl

Questions

What is an eau-de-vie?

The clear distilled spirit before ageing. A cognac blend draws on many of them, of different ages and from different crus, and the blender’s art is in the assembly.

What glass should I use?

A tulip or copita rather than a balloon. It concentrates the aromatics instead of dispersing them, which matters for a cognac this layered.

Why the 35cl format?

It is the same blend as the full bottle in half the measure — a way into Paradis without committing to a 70cl, and a considerably more giftable size.

title: Cipriani Bellini 75cl
descriptionHtml:
Venice · Italy · Bottled Bellini

Cipriani Bellini — white peach purée and Italian Prosecco, from the bar that invented the drink in 1948.

Bottled CocktailItalyWhite Peach PuréeItalian ProseccoHarry’s Bar Original75cl
⭐ Instant delivery across Greater London in 30–45 minutes
⭐ Open 24/7 — every day of the year

The Cocktail

The Bellini was born in 1948 at Harry’s Bar in Venice, and it has been one of the world’s most enduring cocktails ever since. Cipriani, the originator, still makes the definitive version — and this is that drink, bottled.

The recipe is unchanged in principle: the juiciest small white peach purée blended with the finest Italian Prosecco. What you get is effervescent, silky and instantly celebratory, and considerably more refined than the buck’s fizz it tends to replace. No mixing, no measuring — just chill and pour.

Tasting Notes

NoseRipe white peach over fine Prosecco bubbles.
PalateSilky and effervescent, with the peach purée giving weight and texture.
FinishClean and refreshing.

Serve with: brunch, lunch, or an evening gathering. Chill thoroughly and pour into a flute — nothing else required.

At a Glance

Category Bottled Bellini cocktail
Producer Cipriani
Origin Italy
Ingredients Small white peach purée and Italian Prosecco
Heritage Created at Harry’s Bar, Venice, in 1948
Bottle Size 75cl

Questions

Do I need to add anything?

No. It is a complete cocktail — chill it thoroughly and pour.

Why white peach specifically?

White peaches are less acidic and more floral than yellow, which is exactly what the original Harry’s Bar recipe called for. Substituting yellow peach changes the drink entirely.

How should I serve it?

Well chilled, in a flute or a small tumbler as they do in Venice. Give the bottle a gentle inversion before pouring so the purée is evenly through.

Koshitsukano Shuzo has been brewing sake in Niigata for nearly 240 years, and this Daiginjo is the crown jewel of what it makes. Three things underpin it: the brewery’s own home-grown yeast, pristine water drawn from the Agano River, and Yamada Nishiki — the most revered rice variety in sake brewing.

Niigata sake has a reputation for being light and dry. This is the opposite tack: full-bodied and richly textured, with medium acidity giving it shape and a long finish carrying it out. It has the kind of depth that comes from a house doing the same thing carefully for a very long time. 16.5% ABV.

Questions

What makes Yamada Nishiki special?

It has a large starchy centre and low protein, which is exactly what a brewer wants for a highly polished sake. It is the most revered variety in the category, and the hardest to grow well.

What is Daiginjo?

A premium grade requiring rice polished to 50% or less. It produces the most aromatic and refined styles of sake.

Why does the water matter?

Sake is around 80% water, so its mineral profile shapes the finished drink directly. Niigata’s soft snowmelt water is a large part of the region’s reputation.

Late Bottled Vintage was Taylor’s invention. It was launched in 1970 by the firm’s chairman Alistair Robertson, and more than half a century later it remains the benchmark against which every other LBV is judged.

The wine is matured in wood for four to six years before bottling, which does two things: it softens the tannins and it settles the sediment. The Caviar

Beluga is the caviar every other caviar is measured against. Its eggs are prized for exceptional size, a delicate texture that yields rather than pops, and a depth of flavour nothing else in the category reaches. Croe’s Imperial Beluga comes from Huso huso sturgeon, the species indigenous to the Caspian Sea.

The rarity is a matter of biology rather than marketing. A Huso huso takes up to twenty years to reach maturity, so every gram is the product of extraordinary patience and strict sustainable practice. That is why Beluga costs what it does, and why there is genuinely no substitute for it.

A Huso huso sturgeon takes up to twenty years to reach maturity. The cost reflects two decades of husbandry per fish, and the strict sustainability rules that govern the species.

descriptionHtml:

The Wine

Cloudy Bay is the estate that put New Zealand on the fine wine map, and its Pinot Noir is a benchmark for what Marlborough can do with the variety. The fruit comes from the Southern Valleys — cool clay soils on rolling, north-facing slopes, where aged alluvial gravels and dense clay subsoils grow the region’s best Pinot.

It is matured in French oak for eleven months, which is enough to build structure without smothering the fruit. The result is genuinely elegant rather than merely ripe: silky tannins, real aromatic lift, and a long, refined finish. It is also unusually food-friendly, which is a large part of why it has stayed on so many wine lists.

Tasting Notes

NoseDark cherry with wild hedgerow fruits and dusky florals.
PalateElegant and silky, with fine tannins and clear varietal definition.
FinishLong and refined.

Serve with: duck, roast chicken, salmon, or mushroom dishes. Serve at 14–16°C — slightly cool, as Pinot Noir prefers.

Grape Pinot Noir
Region Southern Valleys, Marlborough, New Zealand
Soils Cool clay over aged alluvial gravels, north-facing slopes
Ageing 11 months in French oak

Questions

Why the Southern Valleys?

Marlborough is best known for Sauvignon Blanc grown on the valley floor. The Southern Valleys are cooler, with clay subsoils that suit Pinot Noir far better than the free-draining gravels do.

Should I serve it chilled?

Lightly, yes — 14 to 16°C. Room temperature flattens Pinot Noir; twenty minutes in the fridge sharpens it considerably.

What food suits it best?

Duck is the classic pairing, but it is versatile: salmon, roast chicken and mushroom dishes all work. It is one of the more food-friendly reds on the shelf.

descriptionHtml:

The Whisky

Grain whisky rarely gets to be the main event — in Scotland it mostly disappears into blends. Nikka Coffey Grain makes the case that it deserves better. It is distilled primarily from corn in a continuous Coffey still, the older technology Nikka deliberately retained, and matured in old American oak casks.

The style has no real European equivalent: sweet, tropical and disarmingly drinkable at 45% ABV. Mango, papaya, coconut and candied orange peel sit over a toffee base, and the complexity is there if you look for it without ever announcing itself. It is one of the easiest whiskies in the world to like and one of the more interesting to think about.

Tasting Notes

NoseTropical fruit, vanilla, coconut and candied orange peel.
PalateSweet and mellow — melon, peach, grapefruit and toffee popcorn.
FinishRich oak and marmalade, closing clean and fresh.

Serve with: a little water or a single ice cube, which opens the tropical fruit further. It also makes an excellent highball with soda.

At a Glance

Category Japanese Grain Whisky
Producer Nikka
Base Primarily corn
Distillation Continuous Coffey still
Maturation Old American oak casks
ABV 45%
Bottle Size 70cl

Questions

What is a Coffey still?

A continuous column still patented in the 1830s. It is less efficient than modern equipment, which is precisely the point — it leaves more flavour in the spirit. Nikka kept theirs.

Is grain whisky lesser than single malt?

Different, not lesser. Grain whisky is lighter and sweeter, and it is usually blended away. Bottled on its own at this quality it is a distinct pleasure.

How should I drink it?

Neat with a drop of water, or as a highball with good soda over ice — the Japanese serve, and an excellent one here.

descriptionHtml:

Nikka Miyagikyo — light, delicate and unpeated. Vanilla, apricot, fudge and marzipan from a forested river valley.

The Whisky

Miyagikyo is everything Yoichi is not, and that was the point of building it. Where Nikka’s original distillery sits on a cold northern coast making heavy, peated, maritime whisky, Miyagikyo was sited in a river valley near Sendai — surrounded by forest, with fresh mountain water — to make the opposite.

The result is light, delicate and unpeated: the quiet counterpart to Yoichi’s intensity. Vanilla, apricot, fudge and marzipan sit over a clean fruity base, and at 45% ABV, non chill-filtered, there is more texture than the delicacy suggests. It is the whisky for anyone who finds Scottish single malts too heavy and blends too thin.

Tasting Notes

NoseVanilla, fudge and apricot with a hint of lemon zest.
PalateLight and elegant — lemon, marzipan, gentle oak and soft fruit.
FinishClean, delicate and refreshingly long.

Serve with: a few drops of water, which opens the fruit. It also makes a superb highball, which is how it is most often drunk in Japan.

Questions

How does it differ from Yoichi?

Almost entirely. Yoichi is coastal, peated and powerful; Miyagikyo is inland, unpeated and delicate. Nikka built the second distillery precisely so it could make a different whisky.

What does non chill-filtered mean?

The whisky is not chilled and filtered to remove the compounds that cause cloudiness when water is added. Leaving them in preserves texture and flavour.

Neat with a drop of water, or as a highball with soda over ice — the delicacy holds up better in a highball than most malts would.

Cut Caviar’s Royal Beluga sits at the undisputed summit of the caviar world. The pearls are large and silver-grey, and their defining quality is delicacy — buttery and creamy in texture, dissolving on the palate rather than popping, with a clean, nuanced flavour underneath.

This is the single malt of rum. It was distilled at Guadeloupe’s Bellevue distillery in 1998 and bottled in 2018 — one source, one barrel, individually numbered. What is not in it matters as much as what is: no dyes, no colourings, no cold filtration and no added sugar. The exact, honest age of a distillate matured for two decades.

Why does “no added sugar” matter in rum?

A great deal of rum is sweetened after distillation, which flatters a young spirit and disguises what is actually in the glass. This one is bottled as it came from the cask.

Compounds that make a spirit cloud when chilled — and, with them, texture and flavour. Skipping it preserves both.

Germany’s association of leading wine producers. The barrique used for the finish comes from those estates’ Grand Cru wines.

The Wine

Commanderie de la Bargemone makes Provence rosé with precision at every stage. The vines grow on clay-limestone soils, and the fruit is harvested mechanically at night — cooler temperatures preserve the freshness that daytime picking loses.

From there it is directly cold-pressed, held at low temperature for around ten days, then fermented separately in temperature-controlled stainless steel before the final blend is assembled in December. That parcel-by-parcel approach is why the wine is so precise. Estate-bottled in the Coteaux d’Aix-en-Provence, at 13% ABV.

Tasting Notes

NoseDelicate white flowers and citrus.
PalateElegant and pale, with red fruit and clear definition.
FinishCrisp and refreshing.

Serve with: tapenade, aioli, tapas, barbecue or fish platters — or simply as an aperitif. Serve well chilled, 8–10°C.

At a Glance

Appellation Coteaux d’Aix-en-Provence, France

Blending December

Questions

Why harvest at night?

Cooler fruit arrives at the winery fresher, with less risk of oxidation or premature fermentation. For a pale, delicate rosé that freshness is everything.

What does direct cold pressing achieve?

Pressing whole fruit gently and cold limits skin contact, which is how the wine stays pale and keeps its delicacy rather than picking up colour and tannin.

Why blend in December?

Each parcel is fermented separately, so the final blend is assembled once every component has finished and can be judged on its own terms.

Questions

What does "pure single rum" actually mean?
It is the rum world's equivalent of single malt: 100% pot-still rum from one distillery, with no column-still spirit blended in and nothing added afterwards. Very few estates anywhere still make rum this way — Hampden is the most famous of them.
What is Jamaican "funk"?
The nickname for the intense, fruity, almost solvent-like aroma created by long wild fermentation and high ester counts. In Hampden it reads as pineapple, overripe banana and tropical blossom. It is the most distinctive flavour in rum, and the reason this distillery has a cult following.
Only three years old — is that young?
Not in the tropics. Jamaican heat drives evaporation and extraction several times faster than a Scottish warehouse, so three tropical years deliver a depth of colour and oak you would expect from a far older cool-climate spirit.
Is the charitable donation real?
Yes — £6 from every bottle sold during 2026 goes to relief efforts supporting Jamaica's recovery from storm Melissa. It is one of the rare bottles where the story on the label continues after you buy it.

Why is Michter's so hard to find?
Because the production choices deliberately limit output — low barrel entry proof yields fewer bottles per barrel, batches are small, and nothing is released to hit a date. Demand has grown faster than supply, so allocations are common and shelves empty quickly.
What does "small batch" mean here?
A modest number of barrels selected and married together, rather than hundreds blended for consistency at scale. It means more character in the glass — and slight, welcome variation between batches.
Bourbon or Scotch drinker — who is this for?
Both. It is rich and sweet enough to delight a committed bourbon drinker, and structured enough that a Scotch drinker will take it seriously. If you are buying for someone whose taste you do not know precisely, this is a safe and impressive choice.
Is it good in cocktails or should it be saved for sipping?
Both, honestly. It sips beautifully neat or over a large cube, and it makes possibly the best Old Fashioned you will pour at home. Bartenders reach for it precisely because it does not disappear behind sugar and bitters.

What is a "sherry bomb"?
A whisky matured heavily in ex-sherry casks, which give it dried fruit, chocolate and spice instead of the vanilla and coconut you get from bourbon barrels. GlenDronach 12 is widely regarded as the benchmark entry point to the style — and one of the best value bottles in it.
What is the difference between PX and Oloroso?
Pedro Ximénez is the intensely sweet, raisiny sherry; Oloroso is drier, nuttier and more structured. Using both gives GlenDronach its signature balance — the sweetness of one held up by the backbone of the other.
Is the colour natural?
The depth of colour here comes from twelve full years in sherry wood rather than a short finishing period. Full maturation is slower and more expensive than finishing, and it is why the flavour goes all the way through rather than sitting on top.
Is this a good first serious whisky to gift?
One of the best. It is generous, sweet-edged and immediately likeable, with no peat to divide opinion — but it has enough complexity that an experienced drinker will respect it. The presentation box makes it look the part straight out of the bag.

What does Nc'nean actually mean?

Does organic really change how it tastes?
The bigger influences here are the long fermentation, the mixed yeasts and the red wine casks — those are what give the lemon curd and poached-peach character. Organic barley is a choice about how it is farmed rather than a flavour claim, and the distillery is refreshingly straight about that.
What does "net zero" mean for a distillery?
Nc'nean runs on renewable energy with a biomass boiler burning locally sourced wood chip, and has been verified net zero in its own operations since it started producing. The bottle is 100% recycled glass. No other Scotch distillery started out that way.

Is this too smoky for someone new to Islay?

What does the Pedro Ximénez finish actually add?

Questions

What is the difference between rye and bourbon?
Bourbon is at least 51% corn, which makes it sweet and round. Rye is at least 51% rye grain — this one is 100% — which makes it drier, spicier and more peppery. If you find bourbon a touch sweet, rye is the whiskey you have been looking for.
Is this a sipping whiskey or a cocktail whiskey?
Genuinely both, which is unusual at this age. Ten years of oak give it enough roundness to drink neat, and 100 proof gives it enough backbone that it does not vanish under vermouth and bitters. Most owners do both from the same bottle.
Why is 100% rye harder to make?
Rye is a difficult grain to work with — it foams heavily in the mash and is far less forgiving than corn. Most producers blend in corn or wheat to make life easier. Going all-rye and then ageing it a decade leaves nowhere for a flaw to hide.

Anyone who makes cocktails at home, and anyone who already has the obvious bourbons. It arrives in its own presentation box, and it is the bottle that tends to get talked about when it appears on a bar cart.

Questions

What is a Palo Cortado?
The rarest of the classic sherry styles. A cask marked for fino ageing loses its protective veil of flor yeast unexpectedly and is re-marked — palo cortado, "cut stick". Standard for VORS sherries. The wines are so concentrated that a half-bottle is a generous amount, and it lets the bodega release much older stock at an accessible price. Pound for pound, thirty-year-old wine at this price is one of the best values in the drinks world.

What does "5 Puttonyos" mean?
A puttony is the traditional basket used to carry botrytised aszú berries. The number tells you how many baskets of that concentrated paste went into each barrel of base wine — so five puttonyos is a richer, sweeter wine than three, and closer in intensity to the very top bottlings.
Is it too sweet to drink?

Decades. The combination of high sugar and high acidity makes Tokaji Aszú one of the longest-lived wines in the world — bottles from the nineteenth century are still drinking. It will not go anywhere in your cellar.

What is the difference between cachaça and rum?
Most rum is made from molasses, a by-product of sugar refining. Cachaça must be made from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice, and only in Brazil. That gives it a greener, grassier, more vegetal character — closer to rhum agricole than to a Caribbean dark rum.

All three are fortified, but Madeira is the only one deliberately heated and oxidised during ageing. That process gives it a piercing acidity none of the others have — which is why a sweet Madeira never tastes cloying, and why it survives being open almost indefinitely.
What does Malmsey mean?
It is the English name for Malvasia, the richest of Madeira's four noble grapes. The scale runs Sercial (bone dry), Verdelho, Bual, then Malmsey (sweetest). Malmsey is the one to start with — it is the most immediately generous and the easiest to love.
Does it really keep once opened?
Yes, genuinely. Because the wine has already been through heat and oxidation, air does very little to it. Recorked and kept somewhere cool, a bottle will drink well for a year or more. It is the ideal bottle for someone who wants one glass on a Sunday, not a whole bottle in a night.
Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who likes port but has never explored Madeira, and anyone with a cheeseboard habit. The half-bottle size makes it an elegant addition to a hamper, and the fact that it keeps means it never feels like a burden to open.

Questions

I don't like aniseed — is this still worth trying?
Quite possibly. Anise is the frame here, not the whole picture. With sixty-five botanicals the dominant impression is herbal and spiced — thyme, cardamom, pepper — rather than the flat liquorice hit most people remember from cheap pastis.
Why does it go cloudy?
It is called the louche. The essential oils from anise are soluble in alcohol but not in water, so adding water throws them out of solution and the drink turns opaque gold. It is a sign the oils are real, not added flavouring.
How much water should I add?
Five parts cold water to one part pastis is the Provençal standard. Add the water to the pastis, not the other way round, and skip the ice — it mutes the herbs. Chill the water instead.

Anyone who holidays in the south of France, any cook who makes fish stew, and the drinker who has worked through gin and amaro and wants the next herbal thing. It is also a genuinely striking bottle for the price.

Questions

What does gentian taste like?
Bitter, earthy and faintly floral — closer to a root vegetable than to citrus or herbs. It is the bitterness behind many amari and aperitifs, but here it is the whole point rather than one voice in a chorus.
How bitter is it really?
Assertively, but not aggressively. There is honeyed sweetness and orange peel underneath, and at 20% it is gentle enough to drink before a meal. Anyone who enjoys a Negroni or a grapefruit IPA will be on familiar ground.
What is a White Negroni?
Equal parts gin, Suze and a blanc vermouth, stirred over ice with a lemon twist. Invented in the 2000s and now on menus worldwide — it is the single best reason to keep a bottle of this at home.
Who is this a good gift for?
The home bartender missing one bottle, the Francophile, and anyone who has developed a taste for bitter drinks. The yellow bottle is instantly recognisable and looks striking on a shelf.

Questions

What exactly is Barolo Chinato?
A Barolo DOCG wine infused with china calisaya bark and a set of roots and spices, lightly sweetened and fortified to 16.5%. It sits between a wine and an amaro, and it is a protected Piedmontese speciality rather than a style anyone can make anywhere.
Is it sweet or bitter?
Both, in balance. There is dried cherry and gentle sweetness from the Nebbiolo, then cardamom, rhubarb root and a clean quinine bitterness that dries the finish. It is far less sweet than a port and far less bitter than a hard amaro.
How do I serve it?
A small glass at cellar temperature after dinner, with dark chocolate. In winter Piedmont serves it gently warmed with orange peel. It also makes an excellent substitute for sweet vermouth in a Manhattan.
Who is this a good gift for?
The Barolo drinker who has the wines but not the Chinato, the chocolate lover, and anyone who collects the odd corners of Italian drinking. Pair it with a box of dark truffles and it becomes a complete after-dinner gift.

The Story of the Bodega
What Happens When the Flor Dies
1835
Manuel María González founds his bodega in Jerez. His British agent, Robert Blake Byass, later joins his name to it — and the house has been González Byass ever since.
The Flor
A living cap of yeast that grows on young sherry, sealing it from the air. It is what keeps a fino pale and delicate.
The Choice
Fortify to around 18% and the flor cannot survive. The wine is left exposed to oxygen instead — and begins the slow darkening that makes an oloroso.
The Solera
Barrels stacked in tiers, each drawn from and topped up from the one above, so every bottle carries a trace of much older wine.

Nearly a century later the ban is unwound across Europe, and Pernod returns with a bottling built on its pre-1915 recipe.

The Story of Cristal
The Champagne Made for a Tsar
1876
Tsar Alexander II asks Louis Roederer for a champagne of his own. Fearing assassination, he wants a bottle nothing can be hidden in — so it is made of clear crystal, with a flat base instead of the usual deep punt.
Vintage Only

Estate Grown
Cristal is drawn from Roederer's own Grand Cru parcels rather than bought-in fruit — still unusual in a region where most great houses purchase their grapes.
The 2015
A warm, generous growing season. Riper, rounder fruit than the leaner Cristal vintages, held in line by the chalk minerality the house is built on.

No — this is bone dry. Eden Valley is Australia's home of dry Riesling: all lime, flowers and steely acidity, with none of the sweetness people sometimes expect from the grape.

Yes — Eden Valley Riesling is famous for it. Drunk young it's all fresh lime; given five to ten years under screwcap it develops honeyed, toasty depth while keeping its freshness.

Well chilled at 8–10°C. Its acidity and low-ish alcohol make it one of the best aperitif whites there is — and one of the great matches for spicy food.

Questions

Is Kabinett a sweet wine?
Off-dry rather than sweet. There is some natural residual sugar, but the Mosel's razor acidity balances it so completely that the wine finishes fresh, not sugary — the sweetness reads as ripe fruit.
Why is the alcohol so low?
Kabinett grapes are picked at modest ripeness and fermentation stops early, leaving a little sugar behind. The result is a wine of real complexity at 8.5% — genuinely light, and one of the few fine wines you can enjoy at lunch.
Should I drink it now or cellar it?
Both work, though Prüm is famous for rewarding patience. Young it is taut and citrus-driven; after a decade or two it develops honey, dried apricot and a haunting smokiness. Few white wines age better.
How should I serve it?
Chilled at 8–10°C in a white wine glass. It is superb as an aperitif and one of the very best wines for spicy food.

Questions

What makes this different from modern Rioja?
Most contemporary Rioja is made in French oak for a darker, richer, more international style. López de Heredia never changed course: old American oak, long ageing, hand racking, and release only when the wine is ready. The result is paler, more aromatic and far more savoury — Rioja as it tasted a century ago.
Is Crianza the entry level?
In most bodegas, yes. Here it is relative — Viña Cubillo receives more barrel and bottle age than many other producers give their Reserva, which is why it drinks with a maturity its classification does not suggest.
How does it compare with Viña Tondonia Reserva?
Same bodega, different vineyard and tier. Viña Cubillo is the younger, brighter, more immediately giving of the two; the Tondonia Reserva comes from the estate's flagship vineyard with longer ageing and greater depth. Many people keep both.
Should I decant it?
Worth doing. Half an hour in a decanter opens the red fruit and settles the savoury, leathery notes. Serve at 16–18°C.
Will it age further?
Comfortably. It arrives ready to enjoy thanks to the bodega's long ageing, but well kept it will hold and develop for a decade or more — one reason these bottles are quietly collected.

Questions

Isn’t sherry sweet?
Both sherries here are bone dry. Cream sherry gave the category its sweet reputation, but oloroso seco and palo cortado are dry, savoury wines — closer in spirit to a fine white burgundy than to anything sugary.
How long does sherry keep once opened?
Oloroso and palo cortado are oxidatively aged, so they are far more robust than most wine — recork and refrigerate, and they will hold for several weeks. Fino and manzanilla are the ones to drink quickly.
What is palo cortado?
A rare accident of the cellar: a wine that begins ageing under flor like an amontillado, then loses it and continues oxidatively like an oloroso. The result has the aroma of one and the body of the other. Very little is ever declared.
Should the Tondonia be decanted?
Yes — half an hour, poured carefully off any sediment. Serve at 16–18°C. It arrives ready to drink but will hold and develop for another decade.

The Wine

Caymus Vineyards was founded in Rutherford in 1972 by Chuck Wagner with his parents, Lorna and Charlie Sr., and the family has made Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon every year since. Current releases are known for their ripe, generous style; a 1993 bottle shows what that style becomes with over thirty years of age.

Old Napa Cabernet like this is a different wine from a young release: the primary fruit gives way to dried fruit, cedar and savoury notes, and the tannins soften. It's a bottle for a birth-year gift, an anniversary, or anyone curious how Caymus ages.

Is a 1993 Caymus still good to drink?
Mature Napa Cabernet can drink well at this age, but every old bottle is individual, since its condition depends on how it has been stored. Expect a softer, more savoury wine than a current release.

descriptionHtml:

Only around one cask in ten thousand carries the character to be bottled as Blue Label.

Introduced in 1992 as the summit of the Johnnie Walker range, Blue Label is a recreation of the earliest, rarest blends the Walker family once made. It draws on some of the scarcest whiskies held in the Johnnie Walker reserves — including stock from distilleries that have long since fallen silent. Why is there no age statement?
Blue Label is blended for character, not calendar. Its whiskies are hand-selected from rare reserves for how they taste — some very old, some less so — so a single age number would misrepresent what is in the bottle.

Only around one in every ten thousand casks in the Johnnie Walker reserves has the depth and balance to be used, including whisky from distilleries that no longer exist.

Why This Rosé Is Different
Macerated, Not Blended
The Usual Way
Most rosé Champagne is made by blending a little red wine into white — quick, reliable, and easy to repeat from year to year.

Whole Pinot Noir grapes rest on their skins and the juice is drawn off when the colour is right — the saignée method. It is exacting and unforgiving, and there is no correcting it afterwards.

Questions

What is the robe?
A limited-edition presentation sleeve that dresses the outside of the bottle. Laurent-Perrier has released the Cuvée Rosé in several robe designs over the years, and collectors tend to keep them.
Is the Champagne inside different from the standard Cuvée Rosé?
No. The wine is the same Cuvée Rosé — 100% Pinot Noir, made by maceration, aged at least four years on the lees. What differs is the robe on the outside, which is why the robe editions carry a different price from the plain bottle.
Do you stock other robe editions?
Yes — we also hold the Petal Robe. Each edition is the same Champagne in a different robe, so choose on the design you prefer.
Why is this rosé made differently from most?
Most rosé Champagne is blended by adding red wine to white. Laurent-Perrier instead macerates whole Pinot Noir grapes on their skins and draws the juice off when the colour is right. It is harder to get right and cannot be corrected afterwards, but it gives a more vivid colour and purer red fruit.
How should I serve it?
Chilled to 8–10°C, in a white wine glass rather than a flute — it has enough fruit and body to want the room.
Can you deliver it as a gift?
Yes — enter the recipient's address at checkout and add your message. In London it can be at their door within 30–45 minutes, any hour of the day. The recipient must be 18 or over with ID for our Challenge 25 check.

What does unfiltered mean?

The yeast and proteins are left in rather than stripped out. It makes the beer slightly hazy and gives it a fuller, softer texture and more malt character than a filtered lager.

Why does unpasteurised matter?

Pasteurisation heats beer to extend its shelf life, which dulls the flavour. NOAM is not heat-treated, so it tastes closer to draught — but keep it cold and drink it fresh rather than storing it warm for months.

What is the Reinheitsgebot?

The Bavarian Purity Law, dating from 1516. It restricts beer to water, barley, hops and yeast — nothing else.

The Wine

Cristal was created in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II, who wanted a champagne in clear glass with a flat bottom so no bomb could be hidden in the punt. The clear bottle and the gold cellophane survive; so does the principle behind it, which is that Louis Roederer makes Cristal only from its own grand cru vineyards and only in years it considers worthy. The 2012 is the vintage where that principle went furthest: it is the first Cristal grown entirely on biodynamically farmed estate land.

The blend is 60% Pinot Noir and 40% Chardonnay. Malolactic fermentation is blocked, which keeps the acidity taut and the fruit precise rather than creamy. Around a third of the base wines are vinified in oak, adding texture without flavouring the wine. It then spends a minimum of six years on its lees, and a further eight months settling after disgorgement and dosage. Dosage is 7.5 g/L — dry, but not austere.

A magnum holds 1.5 litres — two bottles — but it is not simply twice as much wine. Champagne houses have known this for a century: the magnum is the format they keep for themselves. For a vintage like 2012, built for the long haul, it is the right glass to be in.

The Wine

Cristal is made only from Louis Roederer's own grand cru vineyards, and only in years the house declares. 2005 was one of the hard ones. The growing season was short and the harvest difficult, with rot pressure in the Pinot Noir, so Roederer leaned harder on Chardonnay than it usually would: the blend came out at 55% Pinot Noir and 45% Chardonnay, with around a fifth of the Chardonnay matured in oak.

What that produced is not the dense, powerful Cristal of a great year. It is a lighter-framed, more supple wine — elegant and airy, with the house's chalky signature intact and an unusually silky texture. Critics who wanted muscle marked it down; those who took it on its own terms found a great deal to like. Two decades on, the early softness reads as maturity rather than dilution, and in magnum it has aged more slowly still.

The Case

Chardonnay is the most planted fine-wine grape in the world and the most misunderstood. On its own it is close to neutral — it has no loud signature the way Sauvignon Blanc or Riesling do. What it has instead is transparency: it takes on the character of the ground it grows in and the way it is handled in the cellar. That is why the same grape can give you something lean and chalky in one village and something golden and buttery three thousand miles away.

This case puts that side by side. Three Burgundies, where Chardonnay is grown on limestone and usually kept away from heavy oak, and one Californian Reserve, barrel-aged and ripe. Three bottles of each means you can open one, learn something, and still have two left.

A Puligny-Montrachet domaine of about fifteen hectares. This is their straight Bourgogne — the same hands that make the village wine, at a fraction of the price.
Nuiton-Beaunoy
A Beaune-based grower partnership drawing on the Hautes-Côtes de Nuits and Hautes-Côtes de Beaune. Stainless steel, aged on its lees. Pear and white peach.
Cave de Lugny
From Lugny in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy, where Chardonnay ripens more fully. Hazelnut, acacia and honey over citrus, with a faintly spiced finish.
Firestone Vineyard
Santa Barbara County, barrel-aged in French and American oak. The richest of the four — golden apple, pear and brioche.

The Wine

Domaine Sylvain Bzikot sits in Puligny-Montrachet, the village that gives white Burgundy its reputation. It runs to about fifteen hectares and is worked by Sylvain and Béatrice Bzikot; the family line traces back to a Polish immigrant who arrived in Burgundy in the 1940s and whose surname is still above the door.

A domaine's Bourgogne Blanc is the wine that tells you most about it. It comes off the younger or outlying parcels, it carries no grand appellation to hide behind, and it is made by exactly the same team in exactly the same cellar as the bottles costing five times more. Here that means a Chardonnay built on citrus and orchard fruit rather than oak — clean, taut and unmistakably Burgundian.

Also in the case. This is one of the four Chardonnays in The Chardonnay Lover’s Case — twelve bottles, three of each, at nearly 10% less than buying them individually.

Questions

What is Bourgogne Blanc?
The regional white appellation of Burgundy — Chardonnay grown anywhere in the region rather than in one named village. It is where the best value in Burgundy usually hides, especially from a good village domaine.
Is it oaked?
Barely, if at all. At this level Burgundy is typically raised in stainless steel or older barrels, so the fruit and minerality lead rather than vanilla and toast.
How does it compare with Californian Chardonnay?
Leaner, higher in acid and more citrus-driven. Californian Chardonnay tends to be riper, fuller and more obviously oaked.
Should I lay it down?
No. Drink it young while the fruit is fresh — within a couple of years is ideal.

The Wine

Nuiton-Beaunoy is based in Beaune and draws its fruit from growers across the Hautes-Côtes de Nuits and the Hautes-Côtes de Beaune — the higher, cooler ground behind the famous slope. Those vineyards ripen later and hold their acidity, which is exactly what you want in a Chardonnay meant to taste of fruit rather than sun.

The Réserve is vinified in temperature-controlled stainless steel and then left on its lees before bottling. No new oak is involved. The lees contact is what gives the wine its weight: it rounds the texture and adds a faint creaminess without ever covering the fruit underneath.

Also in the case. This is one of the four Chardonnays in The Chardonnay Lover’s Case — twelve bottles, three of each, at nearly 10% less than buying them individually.

Questions

What does "aged on its lees" mean?
The wine rests on the spent yeast left over from fermentation. It adds texture and a soft creaminess, and it is how a steel-fermented white gains weight without going anywhere near a barrel.
Where are the Hautes-Côtes?
The higher ground set back from Burgundy's main slope, above the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune. Cooler and later-ripening, which keeps the acidity fresh.
Is it oaked?
No. It is made in stainless steel, so the character comes from the fruit and the lees ageing rather than wood.
What does the Réserve mean here?
It is the producer's own designation for this bottling. In Burgundy "Réserve" is not a legally defined ageing term the way it is in Rioja.

The Wine

Lugny lies in the Mâconnais, the southern end of Burgundy, where the climate is warmer and Chardonnay ripens more fully than it does on the Côte d'Or. The result is a rounder, more open style of white Burgundy — less austere, more immediately generous, and a good deal easier on the wallet.

This is the cuvée the Cave bottles as Eugène Blanc, named for a figure in the co-operative’s own history. You may also see the same wine sold simply as Mâcon-Lugny, which is how the Cave lists it today.

The grapes are gently pressed and fermented in stainless steel, then left on their lees for at least six months with a full malolactic fermentation. That combination is what softens the acidity and builds the texture: this is a Chardonnay with weight and a nutty, honeyed edge rather than a lean and chalky one.

Also in the case. This is one of the four Chardonnays in The Chardonnay Lover’s Case — twelve bottles, three of each, at nearly 10% less than buying them individually.

Questions

Where is the Mâconnais?
The southern end of Burgundy, around the town of Mâcon. Warmer than the Côte d'Or, and the source of most of Burgundy's more affordable Chardonnay.
What does Eugène Blanc mean?
It is the name of this cuvée from Cave de Lugny. The Cave also lists the same wine as Mâcon-Lugny, so you may see it under either name.
What is malolactic fermentation?
A second, gentler fermentation that converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid. It is why this wine tastes rounder and creamier than a Chardonnay where it has been blocked.
Is it oaked?
No. The nutty, honeyed character comes from lees ageing and malolactic fermentation, not from barrels.
How long will it keep?
The producer suggests three to five years depending on the vintage. It is ready to drink now.

Firestone Vineyard was founded in the Santa Ynez Valley in Santa Barbara County, one of the few places in California where the valleys run east to west. That orientation funnels cool Pacific air inland, so the fruit ripens fully in the sun while the nights stay cold enough to hold the acidity. It is why Santa Barbara makes Chardonnay with ripeness and freshness at the same time.

The Private Reserve is the barrel-aged bottling — around ten months in French and American oak, which is where the vanilla, caramel and toasted-brioche notes come from. This is Chardonnay in its full-bodied register: golden in the glass, rounded on the palate, and a world away from the lean Burgundian style.

It is the richer end of the spectrum — barrel-aged, with caramel and brioche notes — but it is built on ripe orchard fruit rather than butter alone.

The white is the one to know. Dry white Bordeaux at this price is usually thin and forgettable; this is neither. The Wine

Pessac-Léognan is the gravel belt on Bordeaux's southern edge, the oldest fine-wine ground in the region and the only part of Graves to carry its own appellation. Wines from here are recognisable: less plush than the Médoc, more savoury, with a smoky, stony quality the French call goût de terroir.

The 2016 Larrivet Haut-Brion is unusual in being led by Cabernet Franc rather than Cabernet Sauvignon, which lifts the aromatics. Critics found truffle, tilled earth and crushed rock over cassis and blackberry, with Provençal herbs underneath. 2016 was one of the great recent Bordeaux vintages, and this is a wine that rewards keeping — it will be on top form from 2027.

Is this related to Château Haut-Brion?

Was 2016 a good Bordeaux vintage?
One of the best of the past twenty years. A dry summer followed by well-timed rain gave wines with ripe fruit and firm, fine tannins built for the long term.

Questions

Is this Echézeaux Grand Cru?
No, and the names are easily confused. Echézeaux is a grand cru in Vosne-Romanée. This is Aux Echézeaux, a separate named plot within Gevrey-Chambertin, several miles north. Different vineyard, different appellation.
Is it Chambertin?
No. Chambertin is a grand cru in its own right. This is Gevrey-Chambertin, the village appellation that takes its name from it — the plot does, however, sit immediately beside the Charmes-Chambertin grand cru.
What is a lieu-dit?
A named parcel of vineyard. Burgundy maps its land in extraordinary detail, and a grower will often bottle one plot separately because it tastes distinct.
How long will it keep?
2021 was a cool, classical Burgundy vintage. It is approachable now and should develop well over the next eight to ten years.

The Hamper

The Chocolate Block comes from Boekenhoutskloof in Franschhoek, and it is the bottle that did more than any other to change how the world looks at South African red. It is Syrah-led, filled out with Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cinsault and lifted by a touch of Viognier — a Cape blend rather than a varietal, built for depth rather than delicacy. Deep ruby, full-bodied, dark-fruited, with spice and a genuine cacao note on the finish that gives the wine its name.

Two bottles is the right number for it. This is not a wine anyone opens carefully over a year; it is a wine that gets drunk the evening it arrives, which is why one bottle so often feels like a mistake.

The chocolate is a box of eighteen truffles from Pierre Marcolini, who opened in Brussels in 1995 and does something few chocolatiers bother with — he buys cocoa at origin and roasts and refines it himself rather than starting from someone else's couverture. The ganache runs drier and more bitter than most, which is exactly what a wine this ripe needs beside it.

It arrives in our cream-and-gold presentation box on shredded tissue, hand-tied with ribbon, and carrying your message on a card.

Questions

Why is the wine named for winds?
Three distinct winds shape Mendoza's vineyards: the cold Polar from the south, the warming Zonda descending from the Andes, and the Sudestada bringing freshness from the Atlantic — together they give the region its distinctive climate for growing Malbec.
How did Malbec become Argentina's signature grape?
It originated in Bordeaux, France, but was brought to Mendoza by a French agronomist in 1868. The region's high altitude and abundant sunshine suited the variety far better than its temperamental homeland climate, and it's now considered Argentina's calling card.
What does "lightly oaked" mean here?
Only a portion of the wine ages in French and American oak for several months, just enough to add structure and spice while letting the ripe, dark fruit character stay the main focus.

Despite the name, Extra Dry is actually slightly sweeter than Brut Prosecco, with more residual sugar — it's one of the most common and approachable styles, ideal as an easy apéritif.
Why is Prosecco made differently from champagne?
Prosecco undergoes its second fermentation in large pressurised steel tanks rather than in the bottle, which is faster and preserves the wine's fresh, fruity character rather than developing the toasty, yeasty notes typical of champagne.
Should Prosecco be aged?
No — Prosecco is made to be enjoyed young and fresh. Unlike champagne, it doesn't improve with cellar time, so it's best bought and drunk within a year or so of release.

Questions

What does "tahona-crushed" mean?
After the agave is slow-cooked in a stone oven, it's crushed by a two-ton volcanic stone called a tahona rather than a modern roller mill — a technique nearly abandoned across the tequila industry until Fortaleza revived it.
Is Fortaleza connected to Sauza Tequila?
Yes — founder Guillermo Erickson Sauza is a direct descendant of Don Cenobio Sauza, who founded the original Sauza Tequila brand in 1873. The Sauza family sold that brand in 1976 but kept the historic La Fortaleza distillery, which Guillermo revived in 1999.
Why no barrel ageing for the Blanco?
Blanco tequila is bottled shortly after distillation specifically to preserve the raw, unfiltered character of the agave itself, rather than letting oak influence the flavour the way Reposado or Añejo styles do.

Why no oak ageing?
The estate keeps this Merlot entirely in stainless steel tanks to preserve its primary fruit character and freshness, rather than layering in oak-driven vanilla and spice from barrel ageing.
What's the story behind the estate?
Bernard and Béatrice Nivollet moved from Paris to the Languedoc in 1995 at 45 years old, deciding to build a wine estate from scratch rather than buy an existing one — identifying individual parcels one at a time before releasing their first vintage in 1998.
Why is it planted on a north-facing hillside?
The cooler aspect, shaded by the hill and surrounding trees, slows ripening slightly and helps preserve the acidity and freshness that define this style of Merlot.

Champagne · Since 1818

In 1956, Jean Roland-Billecart watched his uncle brew beer and had an idea — cold fermentation for champagne. Nearly 70 years later, it's still the house's defining technique.

12% ABV75clNon-Vintage Brut~90% Grand Cru Fruit

Billecart-Salmon may be the only Champagne house that double cold-stabilizes its wine, first at 8°C then 4°C — a slow, six-week fermentation process that preserves purity without needing any synthetic additions.

Questions

What makes the cold fermentation technique special?
Founder's descendant Jean Roland-Billecart introduced it in 1956, inspired by watching his uncle brew beer — a much slower, lower-temperature fermentation than most champagne houses use, which preserves fruit purity and the house's signature freshness.
What is the "perpetual reserve"?
Rather than only blending in wine from a handful of recent vintages, Billecart-Salmon maintains an ongoing reserve dating back to 2006, adding depth and consistency that a purely non-vintage blend wouldn't have.
How should I serve it?
Chilled to around 8–10°C, ideal as an apéritif or paired with delicate dishes like grilled scallops or sushi that won't overwhelm its freshness.

title: La Petite Eglise Pomerol 2018
descriptionHtml:
La Petite Eglise Pomerol 2018 Delivery

Product: La Petite Eglise Pomerol 2018

In the heart of Pomerol, Bordeaux's prestigious Right Bank, Château l'Eglise-Clinet, a historic estate dating back to 1882, crafts wines lauded by critics. Their meticulous approach to viticulture and dedication to quality are evident in every bottle. La Petite Eglise Pomerol 2018, their captivating second wine, whispers the secrets of its grander sibling at an exceptional value. This 2018 vintage is a masterful blend dominated by Merlot (75%), known for its richness and roundness. The Merlot's charm is complemented by the structured elegance of Cabernet Franc (20%), adding complexity and a touch of earthiness. A small inclusion of Cabernet Sauvignon (5%) adds further depth and ensures a long aging potential.

This meticulous composition results in a wine bursting with character, ready to be savored or cellared for future enjoyment. Uncork a bottle of La Petite Eglise 2018 and be greeted by an enticing bouquet. Imagine dark plum and black cherry mingling with earthy notes of graphite, like a whisper of freshly tilled soil. Hints of new leather and menthol add a touch of intrigue, promising a complex and layered experience. The palate offers a beautiful balance of power and grace. The wine boasts a medium-to-full body, with ripe tannins that are firm yet approachable. This structure promises a rewarding evolution in the cellar, where the wine will develop further complexity and nuance for years to come. With lower yields in 2018, this La Petite Eglise is expected to be limited, making it all the more desirable for both seasoned collectors seeking a glimpse into a promising vintage and those new to Pomerol, eager to discover the magic of this esteemed region.

descriptionHtml:

Blended from three highly regarded parcels — Bas de Chapelot, Les Pargues and Cartes-Fontenottes, all adjacent to Premier Cru vineyards — at Samuel Billaud's gravity-fed winery, where the wine is pumped only once and gravity does the rest.

Questions

What does "Les Grands Terroirs" mean here?
It signals that the wine is blended from three separate, well-regarded village parcels rather than a single vineyard — each contributing its own character before coming together in the final blend.
Why is this wine unoaked?
Samuel Billaud reserves oak barrels for his Premier and Grand Cru wines; village-level Chablis like this one is aged in stainless steel and demi-muids to preserve pure, mineral-driven fruit character.
Who is Samuel Billaud?
He spent nearly 20 years as winemaker at his family's estate, Domaine Billaud-Simon, before founding his own label in 2009 — now considered one of Chablis's finest producers in his own right.

descriptionHtml:

The Wine

Harlan Estate sits in the western hills of Napa Valley and has spent decades building a reputation that puts it among the most collected wines in California. The approach is Bordelais in spirit — a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot, aged 24 to 30 months in French oak barrels.

The 2018 pours a dense purple. What lifts it above sheer Napa power is the detail: cassis and blackberry at the centre, then graphite, crushed stone, violets and a curl of tobacco. Medium to full-bodied, it holds power and elegance in genuine balance, with a velvety texture, well-integrated tannins and a very long finish. A wine to keep, and to open for something that matters.

Tasting Notes

NoseCassis, blackberry and black cherry with graphite, crushed stone, violets, cedar and tobacco.
PalateVelvety and layered — dark berries, chocolate and tobacco with earth and subtle spice.
FinishLong and lingering, with spice and vanilla.

Serve with: grilled ribeye, roast lamb, Wagyu beef, savoury mushroom dishes or aged cheeses.

Both work — a long decant opens it beautifully today, and the structure supports many years of further development.

Two to three hours for a wine of this concentration and age.

What temperature should I serve it at?

16–18°C. Serving too warm pushes the alcohol forward and flattens the aromatics.

Its Saint-Estèphe vineyards, close to the Gironde, produce reds of famous structure and longevity. The Cognac

Maison Courvoisier has been making cognac since 1828. This limited edition takes a blend of eaux-de-vie from different crus and matures it in Mizunara oak — the rare Japanese species long treasured by whisky makers for the distinctive aromatics it gives, and notoriously difficult to work into casks.

Questions

What makes Sauternes sweet?

Noble rot — a benevolent fungus that shrivels the grapes on the vine, concentrating sugar, acidity and flavour together. It is unpredictable, labour-intensive and the reason Sauternes is made in such small quantities.

What temperature should I serve it at?

8–10°C, well chilled. Serving it too warm makes the sweetness heavy.

How long does it keep once opened?

Several days in the fridge, tightly stoppered — the sugar and acidity both help preserve it.

Luce 2019 Delivery

Product: Luce 2019

Luce 2019 is a quintessential expression of the Tuscan terroir, born from a collaboration between two winemaking giants: Robert Mondavi and the Frescobaldi family. This iconic wine represents a harmonious blend of Californian innovation and Italian tradition, resulting in a truly exceptional bottle. Founded in 1995, Luce was a pioneering venture that aimed to create a world-class wine from the heart of Tuscany. The 2019 vintage, in particular, is celebrated for its balance and complexity. 

Intense aromas of ripe black cherry and blackberry dominate, complemented by subtle notes of violets and Mediterranean herbs. A touch of spice and cedar emerges, adding depth and complexity to the aromatic profile. The 2019 Luce is full-bodied and structured, with a velvety texture and seamless integration of fruit and tannins. Flavors of dark berries, plum, and licorice are complemented by hints of toasted oak and mineral notes. The finish is long and persistent, with a lingering aftertaste of ripe fruit and spice.  

This adaptable wine goes well with many different types of food. Its deep flavors go nicely with robust pasta dishes with meat-based sauces and grilled red meats like lamb or beef. Luce 2019 is a wine for special occasions. Its elegance and complexity demand a setting that matches its stature. Whether it's a romantic dinner, a gathering of friends, or a personal indulgence, this wine will elevate the experience.

We've also got Château Mouton Rothschild 1985, SGC St. Emilion - Alain Dutournier 2009.
